(1) The setting in which a student performs does not significantly affect the accuracy of his or her performance.

(a) the performance of mildly handicpped students in the special education resource room is not consistent with performance in the regular classroom, and (b) the performance of these students is more variable and less precise when they are tested by a regular classroom teacher using a curriculum probe than when they are tested using a criterion-referenced test administered by a special education teacher in a special education setting.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the extent to which the consistency of performance of handicapped students is affected by changes in the classroom context.
the question of whether or not the instructional materials that handicapped students receive in resource rooms will enable them to perform at the same level when they are in the regular classroom.
the extent to which the consistency of performance of five mildly handicapped students was affected by changes in setting and by changes in test materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of changing settings alone are not as important as the effects of changing curriculum materials.
the results indicate that curriculum differences do have a significant effect on student performance.
curriculum differences, rather than setting changes alone, are the primary factor in the cross-classroom variability of mildly handicapped children's performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
curriculum differences, and not setting differences, are the most important variables affecting the consistency of performance of handicapped students in regular classes.
the results of this study support the notion that handicapped children are able to learn and demonstrate skills in a regular education setting.
, in general, students' performance is more consistent across settings when the same instructional materials are used in both settings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of criterion-referenced materials in a regular education setting can be a useful strategy in the assessment of handicapped students' academic performance in a regular classroom. (Author/CR)
